content: Laryngitis is defined as an inflammation of the larynx, which often results in a hoarse voice or complete loss of voice due to irritation of the vocal folds (vocal cords). The condition is classified as acute if it lasts less than a few days, while chronic laryngitis persists for more than three weeks. Historically, laryngitis has been recognized as an ancient disease. In 1840, Dr. Jordan Roche Lynch, an English physician, documented a case study on the treatment of acute laryngitis. In 2005, Drs. Reveiz, Cardona, and Ospina demonstrated that antibiotics are not effective in treating laryngitis. Laryngitis can be categorized based on symptom duration. Acute laryngitis typically has a sudden onset and is self-limiting, resolving within 3 to 5 days. Chronic laryngitis, on the other hand, is defined as lasting longer than three weeks. The larynx, or voice box, is located at the top of the airway leading to the lungs (trachea) and houses the vocal cords. When the vocal cords become inflamed or infected, they swell, leading to hoarseness and, in some cases, airway obstruction. Laryngitis can result from infectious or non-infectious causes. Viral infections are the most common cause and include rhinovirus, adenovirus, influenza virus, parainfluenza virus, and respiratory syncytial virus. Bacterial causes, though less common, include Staphylococcus aureus and Haemophilus influenzae. It is important to differentiate laryngitis from other conditions such as upper respiratory tract infections, vocal fold cysts, nodules, polyps, or laryngeal stenosis. Acute laryngitis is more commonly observed in children. Women are more frequently affected by laryngitis than men. The incidence of laryngitis is twice as high in winter compared to summer. Risk factors for developing laryngitis include upper respiratory infections, asthma, and exposure to cigarette smoke. Routine screening for laryngitis is not recommended. If left untreated, acute laryngitis generally resolves on its own within 3 to 7 days. Mild throat pain is a common complication. The prognosis for laryngitis is excellent, with no known associated mortality. Symptoms of laryngitis include hoarseness, cough, and swollen lymph nodes. Patients with laryngitis typically appear well during a physical examination. Findings may include vocal fold cysts, nodules, or swollen lymph nodes in the neck. There are no specific diagnostic laboratory findings associated with laryngitis. Imaging studies, such as X-rays, CT scans, or MRIs, do not typically reveal findings directly related to laryngitis. However, imaging may be used to investigate other suspected pathologies. On neck X-rays, findings such as supraglottic or retropharyngeal swelling, unusual narrowing, or soft tissue density in the subglottic airway may be observed. Laryngoscopy is indicated when hoarseness persists for more than two weeks without an apparent benign cause and can be performed via direct or indirect methods. Treatment for viral laryngitis is primarily supportive, as there is no specific antiviral therapy. For infectious causes, antimicrobial therapy is the mainstay of treatment. In cases of laryngitis caused by gastroesophageal reflux, acid suppression therapy with medications such as omeprazole or ranitidine is recommended. Surgery is not a first-line treatment for laryngitis. It is typically reserved for patients with persistent laryngitis due to vocal cord nodules. Primary prevention strategies for laryngitis include avoiding contact with individuals with upper respiratory infections, practicing proper hand hygiene, and smoking cessation. Secondary prevention measures include avoiding throat clearing, increasing fluid intake, and limiting vocal cord usage.
